554.title: The lowest seat (Luke 14:1–14)
554.hook: don't take the top place; invite those who can't repay you
554.howItsDone: Some churches and Christian groups run community meals and soup kitchens open to anyone, and some Christians make a habit of inviting people who are often left out to their own tables, especially at holidays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod the fox and Jesus like a mother hen, wings open over Jerusalem. Your line was under her wings. Who did you reach out to? Day five hundred fifty-four.

A wedding reception. You walk in, and there's no seating plan. Near the head table, a few empty chairs. At the back, by the kitchen door, a table where nobody seems to know anybody. Where do you sit? Luke says Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of one of the chief Pharisees, and he watches the guests come in. He marks how they choose the chief rooms, the best places at the table. And then, being Jesus, he says so.

His advice starts out sounding like ordinary good manners. Don't grab the top place; someone more honored might arrive, and the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom with everyone watching. Instead, in the King James Bible: "go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher." Room there means place, a seat at the table. This wasn't new wisdom. The book of Proverbs says nearly the same thing: don't push yourself forward before the king, because it's better to be told come up here than to be put lower. Jesus is drawing on his own people's old wisdom. But then he lifts it into something bigger: "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." That's not seating strategy anymore. In Jesus' telling, it's how God turns things over. The ones who push up end up down; the ones who go low are called higher. And then he turns to the host, and it gets more uncomfortable. When you give a dinner, don't just invite friends, family and rich neighbors, who'll invite you back. "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." Jesus names the usual habit himself: they'll invite you back, and you'll be repaid. He asks for a guest list made of people who can't pay you back. The repayment, he says, comes later, at the resurrection of the just. Lowest seat for the guest. Open door for the host. Both are about letting go of the score.

Here's the practice: invite someone who can't repay. Settle and breathe. Run through the people you usually share meals or time with. Notice how many of them return the favor; that's normal and good. Now widen the circle. Who do you know, or pass, who rarely gets invited anywhere? An older neighbor living alone. A new coworker. Someone going through a hard time with nothing to offer back. Picture setting a place for them. Then choose one, and decide how you'll invite them: coffee, a meal, a seat at your table. If you pray, you can ask for open doors. The bell holds the time.
The lowest seat. Jesus' advice at a dinner: take the low place, let the host call you higher, and fill your table with those who can't repay.
Your line: friend, go up higher. Today, take the less important seat, the slower line, the last turn, and let someone else go first. Day five hundred fifty-four.

555.title: Excuses (Luke 14:15–24)
555.hook: a field, oxen, a marriage: good reasons to miss the feast
555.howItsDone: Many Christians hear this story as an invitation to worship and to the Lord's Supper, and some churches echo the servant's words when they invite people to the table at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lowest seat, and a host who says friend, go up higher. Did you let someone else go first? Day five hundred fifty-five.

Sorry, can't make it tonight, something's come up. Most of us have sent that message. Some of us have sent it this week. Usually the reason is real enough: work ran late, the kids are tired, we just need a night in. Back at the same dinner table, a guest says something pious and safe: "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." A lovely thought about a feast someday. Jesus answers with a story about a feast right now, and about the very human art of the polite excuse.

A man prepares a great supper and invites many. In that world, guests were often invited ahead of time, then a servant came to fetch them when the meal was ready. That's this moment. The servant goes out with the message, in the King James Bible: "Come; for all things are now ready." The lamb is roasted. The bread is baked. And then: "they all with one consent began to make excuse." All of them. Listen to the excuses, because they're good ones. "I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." The second: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them." Ten oxen, a big purchase; he wants to test them. The third doesn't even ask to be excused: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Land, business, family. Not one of them is a bad thing. Some commentators point out that nobody buys a field without seeing it first, or oxen without trying them, so the excuses may be thinner than they sound. Either way, the effect is the same. The host is left with a feast and an empty hall. He's angry, and then he does something astonishing. Go out quickly, he tells the servant, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind. And when there's still room, go further, out to the highways and hedges. The feast happens anyway. The table fills. The story isn't against fields, oxen or marriages. It's about what happens when good things become the reason we miss the best thing. And in the story the invitation never closes: the servant keeps going out until the house is full.
screen: then, large: `THEY ALL WITH ONE CONSENT BEGAN TO MAKE EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say yes to one invitation. Settle and breathe. Think back over the last few weeks. What did you say no to? A call from an old friend, a community event, a quiet time of prayer you kept postponing, a walk someone suggested. Which of those noes were honest rest, and which were a field and five oxen? Don't judge yourself. Just notice. Then choose one invitation, already waiting or soon to come, and decide now to say yes. If you pray, you can listen for the words: come, for all is ready. The bell holds the time.
Excuses. A field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage: good reasons, given all at once, to miss a feast that was already ready.
Your line: come, for all is ready. Today, when an invitation comes, notice whether your no is honest rest or a field and five oxen, and if it's the oxen, say yes. Day five hundred fifty-five.

556.title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–35)
556.hook: a builder counts the cost before starting a tower
556.howItsDone: Some churches ask adults to prepare over weeks or months before baptism, confirmation or membership, and religious orders give long periods of testing before final vows, so people can count the cost first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, excuses: a field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage, and a feast that filled anyway. Your line was come, for all is ready. What invitation did you say yes to? Day five hundred fifty-six.

Plenty of towns have one. A building that was started and never finished. Concrete pillars with rusting rods sticking out of the top, a fence around it, weeds growing through the foundation. Locals give it a nickname. Kids dare each other to climb it. Drive past, and the thought comes on its own: somebody ran out of money. Jesus uses that same picture at a moment you might not expect, when great crowds are following him down the road.

Luke says great multitudes went with him, and he turned and spoke to them. Not to thank the crowd, but to slow it down. First comes a hard saying: whoever comes to him and does not hate father and mother, even their own life, cannot be his disciple. It sounds shocking, and it should be heard carefully. In the Bible's own way of speaking, hate can mean love less, put second. Genesis says Leah was hated, when the story has just said Jacob loved Rachel more. Matthew gives the same saying plainly: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Read that way, Jesus isn't asking anyone to despise their family; he's saying nothing can come before him. Then the picture: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" Otherwise, he says, you lay the foundation, can't finish, and everyone who sees it begins to mock you: "This man began to build, and was not able to finish." Then a king with ten thousand soldiers facing one with twenty thousand: he sits down first, and counts. Notice the word sits, twice. Discipleship here isn't a rush of feeling at the back of a big crowd. It's a decision made sitting down, with the numbers in front of you. Item by item, add it up. And Jesus doesn't hide the total. Luke ends the passage plainly: whoever does not forsake all that he has cannot be his disciple.
screen: `HATE: A BIBLE WAY TO SAY LOVE LESS.`
then, large: `THIS MAN BEGAN TO BUILD, AND WAS NOT ABLE TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the cost of one commitment. Settle and breathe, and sit down, like the builder. Choose one thing you've said yes to, or are about to: a job, a relationship, a promise to volunteer, a faith practice like this one. Now count, honestly, item by item. What will it take in time each week? In money? In energy, in other things you'll have to give up? Don't let yourself off with a vague answer. When you've counted, ask: can I finish this tower? If yes, recommit. If no, say so now. The bell holds the time.
Count the cost. A builder sits down before starting a tower, adds up what it will take, and Jesus asks the same honesty of anyone who would follow him.
Your line: count the cost. Today, before you say yes to anything new, sit down for one minute and add it up first. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: This man receives sinners (Luke 15:1–10)
557.hook: grumbling leads to three stories of lost things found
557.howItsDone: Christians read Luke 15 often, especially in Lent, and many churches mark returns with celebration: welcoming people back to communion, to membership, or into recovery communities that meet in church halls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a half-built tower and the advice to count the cost before you start. What did your counting show you? Day five hundred fifty-seven.

A sneer, overheard at the edge of a crowd. That's how Luke chapter fifteen begins. The chapter holds a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son, and it's easy to keep the stories and forget why Jesus told them. They weren't bedtime stories, and they weren't told to a quiet audience. They were his answer to a complaint. Luke sets it up in two sentences, and everything after hangs on them. And the complaint itself, meant as an insult, says something true about him.
screen: `A SNEER AT THE EDGE OF A CROWD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." Publicans were tax collectors, and here Luke sets them right beside the word sinners. Sharing a table, in that world, meant accepting someone. So the worry was serious: what does it say about a teacher, about God, if he eats with these people? The Greek word for murmured is a grumbling, muttering word. Some readers hear in it the same word family the old Greek version of Exodus uses when Israel grumbled in the wilderness. Jesus doesn't argue. He tells three stories, and the stakes keep rising. A shepherd loses one sheep out of a hundred. A woman loses one coin out of ten. Tomorrow, a father loses one son out of two. One percent, ten percent, half. And look at how each of the first two ends. Not with the finding. With a party. The shepherd calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost." The woman does the same: "Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." Then Jesus says it straight: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Here's the twist. The grumblers aren't the villains of these stories. They're being invited. Every story ends with someone saying come and celebrate with me. The question underneath the chapter is simple. When the lost come home, will you come to the party? This man receives sinners. It was meant as an accusation. Luke keeps it as a description.
screen: `ONE IN A HUNDRED, ONE IN TEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice over someone's return. Settle and breathe. Think of someone who has come back: to health, to sobriety, to the family table, to faith, to talking to you after a long silence. Maybe the return was small and nobody marked it. Picture them clearly. Notice if any part of you is still grumbling. Let it be there. Then try, just for a moment, to feel the shepherd's joy instead. If you pray, you can give thanks for their return. The bell holds the time.
This man receives sinners. A grumbling accusation that sets up three stories of lost things found, each ending in a party.
Your line: joy in heaven. Today, tell the person who came back that you're glad, out loud, and leave it at that. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: The younger son (Luke 15:11–24)
558.hook: he came to himself, rehearsed a speech, and his father interrupted it with a hug
558.carry: while he was still far off
558.howItsDone: Christians read this story often, especially in Lent; Catholics and Orthodox Christians often connect it with confession, and many churches use it to welcome people who are returning after years away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a grumble, this man receives sinners, and two stories that ended in parties. Your line was joy in heaven. Who did you tell you were glad they came back? Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Have you ever rehearsed an apology? In the car, in the shower, at three in the morning. You polish every line. You plan what you'll say if they shout, and what you'll say if they say nothing. You lower your expectations so you won't be disappointed. Today's story has a young man doing exactly that, on a long walk home. People call it the prodigal son, though Luke never gives it a title. Jesus just begins: a certain man had two sons. Today, the younger one.

The younger son asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is alive. Some commentators say that in that world it was close to saying I wish you were dead. The father divides it anyway. The son goes to a far country and wastes it all. Then famine. He ends up feeding pigs, animals his own people's law counted unclean, and in the King James Bible, "he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him." As low as he can go. Then a turning point: "when he came to himself." Woke up, we'd say. And he works out a speech. "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." And a plan: he won't ask to be a son again, just a worker who gets paid. Then the line that turns the whole story: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." He saw him a great way off. Some readers think he'd been watching the road. And he ran. Some commentators note that grown men of standing didn't run in public. The father doesn't care. The son starts the speech. Father, I have sinned, I'm no more worthy to be called your son. And before he can get to make me a hired servant, the father interrupts, calling to the servants: "Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet." The plan to be a servant never gets said. Robe, ring and shoes: you don't put those on a worker. You put them on a son. And the father says why: "this my son was dead, and is alive again."
screen: `HE RAN, WHILE THE SON WAS FAR OFF.`
then, large: `THIS MY SON WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come back without the speech. Settle and breathe. Is there somewhere you've drifted from? A person, a promise, a practice, a faith. Notice the speech you've been rehearsing for when you go back: the explanations, the bargaining, the lowered expectations. Now picture the father on the road, already running before you've said a word. Let the speech go quiet. If you pray, you can simply turn toward God without the speech, and stay there. If you don't, simply let yourself be welcomed, in your imagination, before you've earned it. The bell holds the time.
The younger son. He wasted everything, came to himself, rehearsed a speech, and was met on the road by a running father who never let him finish it.
Your line: while he was still far off. Today, when someone takes a first step back toward you, run to meet them before they finish explaining. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: The older brother (Luke 15:25–32)
559.hook: the faithful son won't come to the party; the story ends with the father pleading
559.howItsDone: Christians often reflect on both brothers when reading this parable in Lent, and some preachers point to the open ending as a question each listener answers in their own life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the younger son, met on the road while he was still far off, and a speech that never got finished. Did you run to meet anyone? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

Robe, ring, the fatted calf. It would make a fine place to roll the credits. But Jesus keeps going, because the story was never only about one son. Remember the first line: a certain man had two sons. While the party is starting, the older one is still out in the field, working, as he has for years. He comes near the house and hears something coming from inside. Music. Dancing. He calls a servant over and asks what on earth is going on.
screen: `A FINE PLACE TO ROLL THE CREDITS.`

segments.voice: Your brother is home, the servant says, and your father has killed the fatted calf. In the King James Bible: "And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came out his father, and intreated him." Notice that. The father went out to the younger son on the road. Now he goes out again, to the older one in the yard. He leaves his own party to plead. And the older son lets it all out: "Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends." Not even a young goat. The word for serve is the word for working as a slave. He's been at home all along, and living like a hired hand. Then listen to how he names his brother: this thy son. Not my brother. Your son. The father answers so gently. He calls him by a tender word, teknon, child: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." Everything was already his. He never had to earn it. And then the father hands the brother back to him: "It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found." Thy brother. And then the story stops. We never find out if he goes in. Jesus leaves the door open and the music playing. Remember who he was talking to: the people grumbling that he ate with sinners. Some readers hear them in the older brother. Others hear anyone who has been faithful a long time and quietly started keeping score.
screen: then, large: `SON, THOU ART EVER WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to the party. Settle and breathe. Think of a celebration you'd rather skip, because someone is being welcomed or praised who, in your view, hasn't earned it. A colleague's promotion, a sibling's second chance, someone else's easy blessing. Notice the old scorecard come out. Then hear the father's words to his older son: all that I have is thine. What would change if you stopped keeping count? If you pray, you can hold those words for a while. If not, simply imagine walking in through the door, toward the music. The bell holds the time.
The older brother. The faithful son who wouldn't come to the party, a father who came out to plead with him, and a story that ends at the door.
Your line: all I have is yours. Today, go to the celebration you'd rather skip, or send the congratulations, and mean them. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: The shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–13)
560.hook: a puzzling story: use money to make friends; you can't serve two masters
560.howItsDone: Christians use the language of stewardship for money, time and the earth, as things held in trust; many churches teach regular giving, and some Christians keep budgets that set aside money for hospitality and helping others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the older brother stood outside the party while his father pleaded. Your line was all I have is yours. Did you go in? Day five hundred sixty.

It may be the most puzzling story Jesus tells. Even Luke seems to feel the strain: after the story come four or five different morals, one after another. A dishonest employee gets praised. Money gets called unrighteous, then used to make friends. And it comes straight after the prodigal son, with a little clue linking them. The younger son wasted his father's goods. This manager, Luke says, is accused of wasting his master's goods. Same Greek word. Two stories about what we do with what isn't really ours.

A rich man's manager is caught wasting his goods and told to hand in the books. He panics, and in the King James Bible he talks to himself: "What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed." Then he has an idea. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred measures of oil. Quick, write fifty. And you? A hundred measures of wheat. Write eighty. Now when he's out of a job, they'll owe him a favor. And the punchline: "the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely." Not for being honest. For being shrewd, for seeing the crisis coming and acting fast. Scholars genuinely disagree about the details. Some think he cut out his own commission; others think he cut the master's interest; others that he was simply dishonest to the end. What's clear is the lesson Jesus draws: use the money of this world, mammon, to make friends, because people last and money doesn't. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, and Jesus treats it almost like a rival god. Then the line that becomes today's carry: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." Small things train big things. And the closing warning: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master. Look back at the week. The lowest seat. A feast refused with excuses. A tower that needs counting. A grumble that started three stories. A son far off, and another at the door. And now a manager who at least saw clearly that his time was short.
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use money to build a friendship. Settle and breathe. Think about the money that passed through your hands this week: rent, food, subscriptions, things you bought on a whim. Notice which of it made a connection with another person, and which didn't. Now think of one person you'd like to be closer to, or someone who could use a little help. What small amount could turn into a friendship?
